claims.source: As expected, inhibition of mitochondrial uncoupling (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) did not affect mitochondrial content (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) but led to an increase in total ROS levels (Figure 3K)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3K and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B.

claims.claim: Inhibition of mitochondrial uncoupling by siRNA against Ucp2 leads to premature satellite cell differentiation.
claims.source: As expected, inhibition of mitochondrial uncoupling (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) did not affect mitochondrial content (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) but led to an increase in total ROS levels (Figure 3K) and to premature satellite cell differentiation as shown by an increased number of phospho-p38α- (pp38α) and Myogenin-positive cells (Figure 3L, Figure 3—figure supplement 1M).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3L and Figure 3—figure supplement 1M.

claims.claim: Repression of mitochondrial biogenesis by silencing of Tfam leads to a decrease in ROS levels together with delayed differentiation.
claims.source: In contrast, repression of mitochondrial biogenesis by silencing of Tfam (Gleyzer et al., 2005) using siRNA led to a decrease in ROS levels together with delayed differentiation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and E.

claims.claim: Nox2 and Nox4 expression increases in the days (D2-D4) following injury.
claims.source: qRT-PCR analyses indicated that Nox2 and Nox4 expression increases in the days (D2-D4) following injury (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claims.claim: Inhibition of NADPH oxidases by Apocynin leads to a decrease in ROS levels.
claims.source: Inhibition of both enzymes by Apocynin (Petrônio et al., 2013) leads to a decrease in ROS levels (Figure 3M)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3M.

claims.claim: Inhibition of NADPH oxidases by Apocynin leads to an inhibition of differentiation and a maintenance of proliferation.
claims.source: Inhibition of both enzymes by Apocynin (Petrônio et al., 2013) leads to a decrease in ROS levels (Figure 3M), together with an inhibition of differentiation and a maintenance of proliferation, as shown at day 4 by the reduced number of pp38α- and Myogenin-positive cells, and the increased fraction of EdU-incorporating cells, compared to controls (Figure 3N, Figure 3—figure supplement 2G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3N and Figure 3—figure supplement 2G.

claims.claim: Three weeks after injury, Pitx2/3 double mutant mice show severely impaired muscle regeneration with very small fibres, signs of fibrosis, and numerous cells undergoing senescence.
claims.source: Three weeks after injury, Pitx2/3 double mutant mice show severely impaired muscle regeneration with very small fibres, signs of fibrosis, and numerous cells undergoing senescence, in comparison to sections of controls, which display the usual pattern of regenerating centro-nucleated fibres (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Pitx2flox/flox:Pitx3flox/-:mdx/mdx:Pax7Cre-ERT2/+ mice show markedly impaired regeneration with numerous fibrotic areas and three times more cells undergoing senescence than in control mice.
claims.source: In contrast, Pitx2flox/flox:Pitx3flox/-:mdx/mdx:Pax7Cre-ERT2/+ mice, in which both Pitx2/3 genes are specifically invalidated in satellite cells, show markedly impaired regeneration with numerous fibrotic areas and the presence of three times more cells undergoing senescence than in control mice (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Pitx2flox/flox:Pitx3flox/-:mdx/mdx:Pax7Cre-ERT2/+ mice show dramatic muscle loss and premature death.
claims.source: This is accompanied by dramatic muscle loss and premature death of double mutant mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Treatment of Pitx2flox/flox:Pitx3flox/-:mdx/mdx:Pax7Cre-ERT2/+ mice with NAC prevents senescence and the marked aggravation of the dystrophic phenotype.
claims.source: Strikingly, treatment of Pitx2flox/flox:Pitx3flox/-:mdx/mdx:Pax7Cre-ERT2/+ mice with NAC during the whole period (Figure 4C) prevented senescence (Figure 4D) and this marked aggravation of the dystrophic phenotype, leading to a pattern of regeneration and a life expectancy similar to that of controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Mutation of both Pitx2 and Pitx3 in satellite cells leads to altered expression of genes for antioxidant proteins and for the regulator of mitochondrial function NRF1.
claims.source: Consistent with what we observed during foetal myogenesis (L'honoré et al., 2014), mutation of both Pitx2 and Pitx3 in satellite cells leads to altered expression of genes for antioxidant proteins (Mgst2, SelX, SelM, Gstz, Hspb2) and for the regulator of mitochondrial function NRF1 (Gleyzer et al., 2005) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Pitx2/3 deficient satellite cells exhibit an expansion defect.
claims.source: Similarly to what we observed with the Pitx3 mutant, Pitx2/3 deficient satellite cells exhibit an expansion defect (Figure 5B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claims.claim: NAC addition to the culture medium alleviates the expansion defect of Pitx2/3 deficient satellite cells.
claims.source: NAC addition to the culture medium alleviates this phenotype (Figure 5B,C)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claims.claim: NAC exerts a positive effect on control satellite cells by improving both their cloning efficiency and their expansion.
claims.source: NAC addition to the culture medium alleviates this phenotype (Figure 5B,C), and also exerts a positive effect on control cells by improving both their cloning efficiency, probably reflecting improved survival (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), and their expansion (Figure 5B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B, C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Mutation of both Pitx2 and Pitx3 genes leads to a marked reduction in differentiation markers.
claims.source: In contrast to Pitx3-deficient satellite cells, which undergo differentiation following premature cell cycle exit, mutation of both Pitx2 and Pitx3 genes leads to a marked reduction in differentiation markers (Figure 5D,E(i), Figure 5—figure supplement 1G)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D, E(i), and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Mutation of both Pitx2 and Pitx3 genes leads to accumulation of carbonylated proteins.
claims.source: In contrast to Pitx3-deficient satellite cells, which undergo differentiation following premature cell cycle exit, mutation of both Pitx2 and Pitx3 genes leads to a marked reduction in differentiation markers (Figure 5D,E(i), Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), accumulation of carbonylated proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claims.claim: Mutation of both Pitx2 and Pitx3 genes leads to DNA damage marked by γH2AX.
claims.source: In contrast to Pitx3-deficient satellite cells, which undergo differentiation following premature cell cycle exit, mutation of both Pitx2 and Pitx3 genes leads to a marked reduction in differentiation markers (Figure 5D,E(i), Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), accumulation of carbonylated proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D) and DNA damage marked by γH2AX (Bonner et al., 2008) (Figure 5E(ii), Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E(ii) and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Double Pitx2/3 mutant cells do not undergo apoptosis but become senescent.
claims.source: In contrast to the foetal situation (L'honoré et al., 2014), double mutant cells do not undergo apoptosis (data not shown) but become senescent, as evidenced by up-regulation of senescence associated genes (Sousa-Victor et al., 2014) (Igfbp5, Ifitm1 or Ccl5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and by the absence of apoptosis markers.

claims.claim: Double Pitx2/3 mutant cells show an increased number of cells positive for the marker of heterochromatin foci Hp1γ compared to controls.
claims.source: In contrast to the foetal situation (L'honoré et al., 2014), double mutant cells do not undergo apoptosis (data not shown) but become senescent, as evidenced by up-regulation of senescence associated genes (Sousa-Victor et al., 2014) (Igfbp5, Ifitm1 or Ccl5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), and by the increased number of cells positive for the marker of heterochromatin foci Hp1γ (Zhang et al., 2007) (Figure 5E(iii), Figure 5—figure supplement 1G)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E(iii) and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Double Pitx2/3 mutant cells show increased senescence associated β-galactosidase staining compared to controls.
claims.source: In contrast to the foetal situation (L'honoré et al., 2014), double mutant cells do not undergo apoptosis (data not shown) but become senescent, as evidenced by up-regulation of senescence associated genes (Sousa-Victor et al., 2014) (Igfbp5, Ifitm1 or Ccl5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), and by the increased number of cells positive for the marker of heterochromatin foci Hp1γ (Zhang et al., 2007) (Figure 5E(iii), Figure 5—figure supplement 1G) and by senescence associated β-galactosidase staining (Dimri et al., 1995) (SA-βgal, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F), compared to controls.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Culture of double Pitx2/3 mutant cells under 3% O2 does not rescue the mutant phenotype.
claims.source: Culture of double mutant cells under 3% O2 does not rescue the mutant phenotype.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from experimental data.

claims.claim: Treatment of control satellite cells with buthionine sulfoximine (BSO) leads to an increase in ROS levels and senescence.
claims.source: Treatment of control satellite cells purified from Pax3GFP/+ adult mice with buthionine sulfoximine (BSO) (L'honoré et al., 2014) leads to an increase in ROS levels and senescence (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H,I)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H and I.

claims.claim: Excessive ROS lead to apoptosis in foetal muscle cells.
claims.source: suggesting that, while excessive ROS lead to apoptosis in foetal muscle cells (L'honoré et al., 2014), it triggers senescence in adult satellite cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claims.claim: Excessive ROS trigger senescence in adult satellite cells.
claims.source: suggesting that, while excessive ROS lead to apoptosis in foetal muscle cells (L'honoré et al., 2014), it triggers senescence in adult satellite cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing senescence in double mutant cells with high ROS levels.

claims.claim: Treatment of double Pitx2/3 mutant cells with NAC efficiently prevents DNA damage.
claims.source: Treatment of double mutant cells with NAC efficiently prevents DNA damage (Figure 5E(ii), Figure 5—figure supplement 1G)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E(ii) and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Treatment of double Pitx2/3 mutant cells with NAC prevents protein carbonylation.
claims.source: Treatment of double mutant cells with NAC efficiently prevents DNA damage (Figure 5E(ii), Figure 5—figure supplement 1G) and protein carbonylation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claims.claim: Treatment of double Pitx2/3 mutant cells with NAC results in markedly fewer senescent cells.
claims.source: Treatment of double mutant cells with NAC efficiently prevents DNA damage (Figure 5E(ii), Figure 5—figure supplement 1G) and protein carbonylation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D), resulting in markedly fewer senescent cells (Figure 5E(iii), Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E(iii) and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, G.

claims.claim: Treatment of double Pitx2/3 mutant cells with NAC results in the restoration of their differentiation potential.
claims.source: Treatment of double mutant cells with NAC efficiently prevents DNA damage (Figure 5E(ii), Figure 5—figure supplement 1G) and protein carbonylation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D), resulting in markedly fewer senescent cells (Figure 5E(iii), Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G), and in the restoration of their differentiation potential (Figure 5E(i), Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E(i) and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Treatment of double Pitx2/3 mutant cells with SB203580 efficiently reduces senescence.
claims.source: Treatment with SB203580 efficiently reduces senescence (Figure 5E(iii), Figure 5—figure supplement 1G)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E(iii) and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Treatment of double Pitx2/3 mutant cells with SB203580 does not rescue DNA damage.
claims.source: Treatment with SB203580 efficiently reduces senescence (Figure 5E(iii), Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), but does not rescue DNA damage (Figure 5E(ii), Figure 5—figure supplement 1G)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E(ii) and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Treatment of double Pitx2/3 mutant cells with SB203580 results in impairment of differentiation.
claims.source: Treatment with SB203580 efficiently reduces senescence (Figure 5E(iii), Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), but does not rescue DNA damage (Figure 5E(ii), Figure 5—figure supplement 1G) with consequent impairment of differentiation (Figure 5E(i), Figure 5—figure supplement 1G) (Puri et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E(i) and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: The excessive ROS levels in Pitx2/3 double mutant satellite cells are responsible for their senescence due to protein oxidation and DNA damage.
claims.source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that the excessive ROS levels observed in Pitx2/3 double mutant satellite cells are responsible for their senescence, due to protein oxidation and DNA damage
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that NAC treatment prevents senescence, protein oxidation, and DNA damage.

claims.claim: NAC treatment alone leads to a reduction in p38α MAP kinase phosphorylation in cultured satellite cells.
claims.source: Immunostaining experiments (Figure 6A) show that while NAC or SB treatment alone leads to a reduction in p38α MAP kinase phosphorylation, the NAC/SB combination has a more pronounced effect on p38α MAP kinase phosphorylation and therefore activation of this signalling pathway.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: SB treatment alone leads to a reduction in p38α MAP kinase phosphorylation in cultured satellite cells.
claims.source: Immunostaining experiments (Figure 6A) show that while NAC or SB treatment alone leads to a reduction in p38α MAP kinase phosphorylation, the NAC/SB combination has a more pronounced effect on p38α MAP kinase phosphorylation and therefore activation of this signalling pathway.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The NAC/SB combination has a more pronounced effect on p38α MAP kinase phosphorylation than NAC or SB alone.
claims.source: Immunostaining experiments (Figure 6A) show that while NAC or SB treatment alone leads to a reduction in p38α MAP kinase phosphorylation, the NAC/SB combination has a more pronounced effect on p38α MAP kinase phosphorylation and therefore activation of this signalling pathway.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: NAC and SB treatments both reduce differentiation of satellite cells in culture.
claims.source: Accordingly, while NAC and SB treatments, under which proliferation is promoted (Figure 6B,C), both reduce differentiation (Figure 6D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Treatment with the dual NAC/SB combination leads to even stronger effects on reducing differentiation than NAC or SB alone.
claims.source: Accordingly, while NAC and SB treatments, under which proliferation is promoted (Figure 6B,C), both reduce differentiation (Figure 6D), treatment with the dual NAC/SB combination leads to even stronger effects (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: After 3 days of culture in control conditions, only 40% of satellite cells show EdU incorporation.
claims.source: Indeed, whereas after 3 days of culture in control conditions only 40% of cells show EdU incorporation, treatment with the NAC/SB combination leads to a major increase, with 80% of cells positive for EdU (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A(i)).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A(i).

claims.claim: Treatment with the NAC/SB combination leads to 80% of satellite cells being positive for EdU after 3 days of culture.
claims.source: Indeed, whereas after 3 days of culture in control conditions only 40% of cells show EdU incorporation, treatment with the NAC/SB combination leads to a major increase, with 80% of cells positive for EdU (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A(i)).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A(i).

claims.claim: NAC/SB treatment promotes a 10 fold increased expansion of satellite cells compared to controls in clonal analysis.
claims.source: Clonal analysis shows that this strong proliferative activity promotes a 10 fold increased expansion compared to controls, with a mean number of 250 cells per clone compared to 25 (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: After 3 days of culture, NAC/SB-treated satellite cells do not show p21 and Myogenin expression.
claims.source: After 3 days of culture, NAC/SB-treated cells do not show p21 and Myogenin expression (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: NAC/SB-treated satellite cells retain a high level of Pax7 expression after 3 days of culture.
claims.source: After 3 days of culture, NAC/SB-treated cells do not show p21 and Myogenin expression (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and retain a high level of Pax7 expression (data not shown)
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from experimental data.

claims.claim: Culturing satellite cells in 3% O2 does not substitute for NAC treatment.
claims.source: Similar results were obtained when cells were cultured in 3% O2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C), showing that conditions considered as normoxic do not substitute for NAC.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C.

claims.claim: Satellite cells cultured under standard conditions display a regenerative potential at least 10 times lower than freshly isolated satellite cells in grafting experiments.
claims.source: While satellite cells cultured under standard conditions display a regenerative potential at least 10 times lower than freshly isolated satellite cells (Montarras et al., 2005) (Figure 6F,G)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F and G, and by a citation to published literature.

claims.claim: NAC/SB treatment of cultured satellite cells leads to very efficient engraftment, with a number of Dystrophin-positive cells similar to that obtained with freshly isolated satellite cells.
claims.source: While satellite cells cultured under standard conditions display a regenerative potential at least 10 times lower than freshly isolated satellite cells (Montarras et al., 2005) (Figure 6F,G), NAC/SB treatment of cultured satellite cells leads to a very efficient engraftment, with a number of Dystrophin-positive cells similar to that obtained with freshly isolated satellite cells (Figure 6F,G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F and G.

claims.claim: Transplanted satellite cells treated with NAC/SB successfully populate the satellite cell compartment in recipient muscles.
claims.source: To test whether engrafted cells also contributed to the satellite cell compartment in recipient muscles, we performed immunostaining with GFP and Pax7 antibodies. Both staining co-localized in a subset of nuclei in the engrafted muscle, indicating that the transplanted cells also successfully populated the satellite cell compartment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1J.

claims.claim: Donor satellite cells treated with both NAC and SB203580 are much more abundant (x20) after injury than when treated with NAC or SB alone (x2).
claims.source: Injury regeneration assays performed 3 weeks after grafting (Figure 6H–K) show that donor satellite cells treated with both NAC and SB203580 are much more abundant, (x20, Figure 6K) than when treated with NAC or SB alone, which also have a positive effect compared to controls (x2, Figure 6I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I and K.

claims.claim: NAC or SB treatments both improve the regeneration potential of cultured satellite cells in grafting experiments.
claims.source: In addition, this grafting analysis (Figure 6J,K) further indicates that while NAC or SB treatments both improve the regeneration potential of cultured satellite cells (Figure 6J,K)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6J and K.

claims.claim: The use of both NAC and SB compounds leads to a much higher number of Dystrophin-positive fibres in grafting experiments.
claims.source: In addition, this grafting analysis (Figure 6J,K) further indicates that while NAC or SB treatments both improve the regeneration potential of cultured satellite cells (Figure 6J,K), the use of both compounds leads to a much higher number of Dystrophin-positive fibres (Figure 6J,K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6J and K.

claims.claim: Cells treated with both NAC and SB compounds display a higher regeneration potential and a much higher capacity to expand and self-renew upon grafting.
claims.source: Taken together, these results indicate that cells treated with both compounds display a higher regeneration potential, together with a much higher capacity to expand and self-renew upon grafting.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from grafting experiments.

claims.claim: Pitx2 and Pitx3 factors are involved in the redox control of the muscle satellite cell.
claims.source: As during foetal myogenesis, we show that Pitx2/3 factors are involved in the redox control of the muscle satellite cell.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing altered ROS levels in Pitx2/3 mutant satellite cells.

claims.claim: The link between Pitx factors and the control of ROS has been reported in cardiomyocytes where Pitx2 plays a critical role in the regulation of antioxidant scavenger genes.
claims.source: The link between Pitx factors and the control of ROS has also been reported in cardiomyocytes where Pitx2, the only Pitx gene expressed in the heart, plays a critical role in the regulation of antioxidant scavenger genes (Tao et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claims.claim: In the absence of Pitx3 alone, the balance between proliferation and differentiation is perturbed so that satellite cells differentiate prematurely.
claims.source: In the absence of Pitx3 alone, the balance between proliferation and differentiation is perturbed so that satellite cells differentiate prematurely, a phenotype that impacts the efficiency of muscle regeneration.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing premature differentiation markers in Pitx3 mutant satellite cells.

claims.claim: ROS are now established as important regulators of signalling pathways.
claims.source: Although historically viewed as harmful, ROS are now established as important regulators of signalling pathways (Bigarella et al., 2014; Holmström and Finkel, 2014; Khacho and Slack, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: The increase in ROS occurring in proliferating satellite cells leads to activation of p38α MAP kinase.
claims.source: Using chemical as well as genetic manipulation of the redox state of satellite cells during muscle regeneration, we show that the increase in ROS occurring in proliferating satellite cells leads to activation of p38α MAP kinase
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that ROS scavengers prevent p38α MAP kinase activation.

claims.claim: Redox activation of p38α MAP kinase is linked to its function as a critical regulator of satellite cell differentiation.
claims.source: Using chemical as well as genetic manipulation of the redox state of satellite cells during muscle regeneration, we show that the increase in ROS occurring in proliferating satellite cells leads to activation of p38α MAP kinase and link this redox activation to its function as a critical regulator of satellite cell differentiation (Segalés et al., 2016; Perdiguero et al., 2007; Brien et al., 2013; Palacios et al., 2010) (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to published literature.

claims.claim: ROS levels affect satellite cell behaviour independently of p38α MAP kinase.
claims.source: Given the striking synergistic effect that we observe with NAC which lowers ROS levels and SB which inhibits p38α MAP kinase, it is probable that ROS levels also affect satellite cell behaviour independently of p38α MAP kinase.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the synergistic effects observed with NAC and SB treatment.

claims.claim: In the double Pitx2/3 mutant, DNA damage is reversed by NAC treatment but not by SB, indicating that DNA damage reflects a p38α-independent effect of high ROS levels.
claims.source: This is demonstrated by our analysis of the double Pitx2/3 mutant, where DNA damage is reversed by NAC treatment but not by SB, indicating that they reflect a p38α−independent effect of high ROS levels.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing differential effects of NAC and SB on DNA damage.

claims.claim: In wild-type satellite cells, cloning efficiency is improved by NAC but not SB treatment.
claims.source: In wild-type satellite cells too, cloning efficiency is improved by NAC but not SB treatment suggesting that lowering ROS levels in normal cells also reduces a background level of DNA damage.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing improved cloning efficiency with NAC treatment.

claims.claim: The striking effect of NAC and SB together may reflect reduced DNA damage due to ROS and delayed differentiation.
claims.source: The striking effect of NAC and SB together may reflect reduced DNA damage due to ROS, which will repercuss on the cell cycle, as well as delayed differentiation (Shaltiel et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed synergistic effects and a citation to published literature.

claims.claim: ROS are mainly generated by the mitochondrial respiratory chain and by NADPH oxidases.
claims.source: ROS are mainly generated by the mitochondrial respiratory chain and by NADPH oxidases (Murphy, 2009; Katsuyama et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: A peak of mitochondrial ROS production occurs at day 2 of regeneration, when mitochondrial mass is only beginning to increase in activated satellite cells.
claims.source: We show that a peak of mitochondrial ROS production occurs at day 2 of regeneration, when mitochondrial mass is only beginning to increase in activated satellite cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing ROS and mitochondrial mass measurements at different time points.

claims.claim: Under conditions in which the cellular energy demand is still moderate, increased ROS production has been reported to occur from complex I.
claims.source: Under conditions in which the cellular energy demand is still moderate, increased ROS production has been reported to occur from complex I (Murphy, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claims.claim: NADPH oxidases contribute to the redox state of satellite cells and the regulation of satellite cell differentiation.
claims.source: In addition to mitochondrial ROS, by using Apocynin, an inhibitor of NADPH oxidases (Petrônio et al., 2013), we demonstrate a contribution of these enzymes to the redox state of satellite cells and the regulation of satellite cell differentiation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data using Apocynin treatment.

claims.claim: Extracellular sources of ROS released into the environment by injured muscle fibres and inflammatory cells will also contribute to the in vivo scenario.
claims.source: In this study we have focused on the cell-autonomous role of the satellite cell redox state, but extracellular sources of ROS released into the environment by injured muscle fibres and inflammatory cells (Le Moal et al., 2017), will also contribute to the in vivo scenario.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of the regeneration environment and a citation to published literature.

claims.claim: The metabolic switch that accompanies the satellite cell transition from quiescence to ex vivo activation results in a decrease of intracellular NAD(+) levels and of the activity of the histone deacetylase, Sirt1.
claims.source: The metabolic switch that accompanies the satellite cell transition from quiescence to ex vivo activation (Ryall et al., 2015) results in a decrease of intracellular NAD(+) levels and of the activity of the histone deacetylase, Sirt1, leading to elevated H4K16 acetylation and activation of muscle genes required for the entry of satellite cells into the myogenic program (Ryall et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Sirt1 has been shown to be critical for the maintenance of hematopoietic stem cells.
claims.source: In the hematopoietic system, Sirt1 has been shown to be critical for the maintenance of hematopoietic stem cells (Matsui et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Sirt1 has been characterized as a direct redox sensor, which is inactivated upon oxidation of its cysteine residues.
claims.source: In addition, Sirt1 has been characterized as a direct redox sensor, which is inactivated upon oxidation of its cysteine residues (Zee et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Increased ROS levels during normal regeneration may lead to Sirt1 inactivation in parallel with activation of p38α MAP kinase.
claims.source: It is therefore possible that increased ROS levels during normal regeneration lead to Sirt1 inactivation in parallel with activation of p38α MAP kinase, and consequent onset of differentiation.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the known properties of Sirt1 and the observed effects of ROS.

claims.claim: In skeletal muscle, ageing is accompanied by a decline in regenerative capacity.
claims.source: In skeletal muscle, as in many tissues, ageing is accompanied by a decline in regenerative capacity (Sousa-Victor et al., 2014; Cosgrove et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: The aged systemic environment significantly impacts the function of satellite cells.
claims.source: While the aged systemic environment significantly impacts the function of satellite cells (Gopinath and Rando, 2008)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Impaired regeneration in aged muscle is also due to a cell-autonomous functional decline in satellite cells.
claims.source: recent studies have shown that impaired regeneration is also due to a cell-autonomous functional decline in satellite cells (Sousa-Victor et al., 2014; Cosgrove et al., 2014; Bernet et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Geriatric satellite cells have been shown to have elevated p38α MAP kinase activity.
claims.source: Geriatric satellite cells have been shown to have elevated p38α MAP kinase activity (Cosgrove et al., 2014; Bernet et al., 2014)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Geriatric satellite cells have defective autophagy leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and excessive ROS levels.
claims.source: Geriatric satellite cells have been shown to have elevated p38α MAP kinase activity (Cosgrove et al., 2014; Bernet et al., 2014) and defective autophagy leading to mitochondrial dysfunction, excessive ROS levels (García-Prat et al., 2016)

claims.claim: Geriatric satellite cells show increased DNA damage and senescence.

results.result: Satellite cell activation during muscle regeneration is accompanied by metabolic changes including increased mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative phosphorylation, leading to elevated ROS production that peaks at day 2-3 post-injury, prior to differentiation onset.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C12-C13, C15-C18, C20-C23 collectively demonstrate through transcriptome analysis, Seahorse metabolic assays, and flow cytometry measurements that satellite cells undergo a metabolic shift from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation during activation, with corresponding increases in mitochondrial mass and ROS levels peaking before differentiation markers appear. The temporal correlation and multiple independent measurements provide strong converging evidence.

results.result: Pitx3 mutant satellite cells exhibit moderately elevated ROS levels leading to premature differentiation, reduced proliferation, and impaired muscle regeneration with fiber hypoplasia and satellite cell depletion after repeated injury.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C26, C28, C30-C38 demonstrate through in vivo regeneration studies, immunofluorescence, and EdU incorporation assays that Pitx3 loss causes moderate ROS elevation (C26), premature differentiation markers (C32-C33), reduced proliferation (C32), and progressive regeneration defects (C35-C37). The phenotype is consistent across single injury, repeated injury, and dystrophic contexts.

results.result: Pitx2/3 double mutant satellite cells show excessive ROS levels causing senescence, DNA damage, and severe regeneration failure, which is prevented by NAC treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C27, C58-C61 demonstrate through multiple injury models and senescence markers that double Pitx2/3 mutation causes very high ROS (C27), senescence (C58-C59), premature death (C60), and that NAC treatment rescues these phenotypes (C61). The rescue experiment provides strong causal evidence linking excessive ROS to the observed pathology.

results.result: Physiological ROS increase is required for satellite cell differentiation through redox activation of p38α MAP kinase, as demonstrated by NAC and p38α inhibitor preventing premature differentiation in Pitx3 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C39-C49 establish through pharmacological (NAC, Trolox, SB203580) and genetic (siRNA) interventions that ROS elevation activates p38α MAP kinase (C45, C48), which drives differentiation (C46-C47, C49). The convergence of multiple independent inhibition approaches and rescue of the Pitx3 mutant phenotype (C42-C43) provides strong mechanistic evidence.

results.result: Both mitochondrial and NADPH oxidase-derived ROS contribute to satellite cell differentiation, as shown by manipulation of Ucp2, Tfam, and Nox enzymes affecting ROS levels and differentiation timing.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C57 demonstrate through siRNA knockdown (Ucp2, Tfam) and pharmacological inhibition (Apocynin) that both mitochondrial uncoupling (C52-C53), mitochondrial biogenesis (C54), and NADPH oxidases (C55-C57) regulate ROS levels and differentiation. TNFα experiments (C50-C51) further confirm ROS-dependent effects. Multiple independent manipulations converge on the same conclusion.

results.result: Pitx2/3 double mutant satellite cells exhibit altered antioxidant gene expression, excessive ROS, protein carbonylation, DNA damage, and senescence rather than differentiation, all of which are rescued by NAC treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C71, C73, C75-C79 demonstrate through qPCR, oxyblot, γH2AX staining, and senescence markers that double mutants have dysregulated antioxidant genes (C62), expansion defects (C63-C64), reduced differentiation (C66), protein oxidation (C67), DNA damage (C68), and multiple senescence markers (C69-C71, C73). NAC rescue of all phenotypes (C76-C79) provides strong causal evidence.

results.result: p38α MAP kinase inhibition reduces senescence in Pitx2/3 double mutants but does not rescue DNA damage or differentiation, indicating ROS effects are partially p38α-independent.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C83 show through SB203580 treatment that p38α inhibition reduces senescence (C80) but not DNA damage (C81), resulting in impaired differentiation (C82). This differential response compared to NAC (which rescues both) demonstrates p38α-independent ROS effects (C83), providing important mechanistic insight into the pathway.

results.result: Combined NAC and p38α inhibitor (SB203580) treatment produces synergistic effects on satellite cell expansion in culture, with 80% EdU incorporation, 10-fold increased clone size, and maintained undifferentiated state.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C84-C93 demonstrate through multiple assays (EdU incorporation, clonal analysis, differentiation markers) that NAC/SB combination produces stronger effects than either alone (C86, C88), achieving 80% proliferation (C89-C90), 10-fold expansion (C91), and blocking differentiation (C92-C93). The synergistic effect is well-documented across multiple independent measurements.

results.result: NAC/SB203580-treated cultured satellite cells maintain regenerative potential equivalent to freshly isolated cells in transplantation assays, with 20-fold greater donor cell abundance after injury compared to single treatments.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C95-C101, C131-C132 demonstrate through transplantation into dystrophic mice that NAC/SB treatment rescues the typical 10-fold loss of regenerative potential in cultured cells (C95-C96), enables satellite cell compartment repopulation (C97), and produces 20-fold more donor cells after injury than single treatments (C98). Multiple grafting experiments with quantification provide strong functional validation.

results.result: Pitx2 and Pitx3 transcription factors regulate satellite cell redox state, with Pitx3 loss causing premature differentiation and both factors being upregulated during satellite cell activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C24-C25, C102-C104 establish through prior work (C14), expression analysis (C24), and mutant phenotypes (C25, C104) that Pitx2/3 regulate redox state in satellite cells. The similar role in cardiomyocytes (C103) provides independent validation. However, the mechanistic details of how these transcription factors regulate ROS are not fully elucidated in the current work.

results.result: ROS activate p38α MAP kinase to regulate differentiation, but also have p38α-independent effects on DNA damage and cell survival, as evidenced by differential responses to NAC versus SB203580.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C111 establish through comparative analysis of NAC and SB203580 effects that ROS activate p38α (C106-C107) but also act independently (C108-C109). The differential rescue of DNA damage by NAC but not SB (C109-C110) and synergistic effects (C111) provide strong evidence for parallel pathways. The mechanistic dissection is well-supported.

results.result: Culturing satellite cells at 3% O2 (normoxic conditions) does not rescue Pitx3 mutant phenotypes or substitute for NAC treatment effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C44, C72, C94 demonstrate through parallel culture experiments that 3% O2 does not rescue mutant phenotypes (C44, C72) or replicate NAC effects (C94). This control experiment strengthens the conclusion that the observed effects are due to specific ROS modulation rather than general oxygen tension, though the biological interpretation could be more nuanced.

results.result: Mitochondrial ROS production peaks at day 2 of regeneration when mitochondrial mass is still increasing, with contributions from complex I and NADPH oxidases, plus potential extracellular ROS sources.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C116 establish the timing and sources of ROS production through direct measurements (C113) and literature support for complex I (C114) and NADPH oxidases (C115). The acknowledgment of extracellular sources (C116) is appropriately cautious. The temporal dissociation between ROS peak and mitochondrial mass increase is an important observation.

results.result: Metabolic switching during satellite cell activation may involve Sirt1 inactivation through ROS-mediated oxidation, potentially acting in parallel with p38α MAP kinase activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C120 propose a connection between ROS, Sirt1, and differentiation based on literature (C117-C119) and speculation (C120). While the hypothesis is plausible and well-reasoned, no direct experimental evidence for Sirt1 involvement in the current system is provided. This represents an interesting mechanistic hypothesis requiring future validation.

results.result: Aged satellite cells exhibit elevated p38α activity, defective autophagy, excessive ROS, DNA damage, and senescence, with Pitx2/3 mutants proposed as a model of premature muscle aging.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C127 draw parallels between aging phenotypes (C121-C126, all from literature) and Pitx2/3 mutants (C127). While the phenotypic similarities are noted, the proposal that Pitx2/3 mutants model premature aging (C127) is speculative and lacks direct experimental validation such as comparison with aged satellite cells or molecular aging markers.

results.result: Background and context claims establishing satellite cell biology, ROS signaling, metabolic regulation, and prior therapeutic approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C9-C11, C19, C105, C112, C128-C130 provide established background knowledge from literature citations. These contextual claims are well-supported by the cited references and represent accepted knowledge in the field, appropriately framing the current work.
